Angular applications rarely become difficult because of the framework itself. They become difficult because every component eventually starts making its own rogue architectural decisions.
In a single codebase, you’ll often find one component using RxJS for local state, another relying entirely on Signals, and a third mixing both unpredictably. Subscriptions pile up, change detection becomes a black box, and component state lives everywhere. Months later, introducing a minor feature requires surgical changes across five different files.
The framework isn’t the problem. Architectural inconsistency is.
Let’s look at the anti-patterns that slowly turn Angular projects into maintenance nightmares — and how experienced developers avoid them.
1. Stop Treating Signals as an RxJS Replacement
A major misconception in the modern Angular ecosystem is that Signals are here to completely replace RxJS. Forcing one into the other’s territory leads to awkward, brittle code.
// ❌ The Anti-Pattern: Treating RxJS observables like Signals
user$ = this.http.get<User>('/api/user');
name = computed(() => this.user$().name); // This will not compile because Observables are not Signals.Signals excel at synchronous, local UI state tracking. RxJS excels at asynchronous, event-driven streams (like HTTP requests, debouncing, and WebSocket connections).
